name: Cerulean Tithe

detectability.signature: A blue-white ring of compressed starlight; gravimetric pings return exactly twice, once from each mouth.

proximity: Compass headings oscillate between two stellar frames
Long-range comms echo with a half-second doubling
contact: Transit shudders the hull as local space pinches through the throat
Ships exit several light-seconds off their plotted vector
prolonged_exposure: Repeated transits leave crews with persistent double memories of the same voyage
Hull metallurgy shows crystalline fatigue from accumulated spacetime shear

phenomena: Light bending around the throat in a cerulean ring
Objects accelerating without thrust as they near either mouth
Tidal forces causing structural stress at the peak of each pulse
hazards: Structural collapse from tidal forces at pulse maximum
opportunities: Shortcut through normal space cutting forty years off the deep lane
Strategic chokepoint control contested by three trade cartels
Access to otherwise unreachable regions beyond the galactic ridge
known_incidents: The liner Vesper of Ruins exited sixty light-years off-course in 2288, all passengers two days older than their manifest.
Cartel skirmishes at the northern mouth in 2302 ended abruptly when both squadrons emerged from the southern one simultaneously.
description: Cerulean Tithe appears as a ring of bent blue light hanging between two empty coordinates, its throat a disc of compressed stars. Gravimetric sweeps return a doubled signature, one echo from each mouth, thirty-one hours out of phase. To the eye it resembles a tollgate built by no one.

The aperture breathes on a 31-hour cycle, dilating wide enough for capital tonnage at peak and narrowing to a needle at trough. Objects drifting near either mouth accelerate gently toward the throat without any thrust at all. Transit is survivable but rough; hulls emerge humming, and exit points wander by light-seconds pulse to pulse.

Deep survey teams found the paired mouths in 2261 while chasing a duplicated pulsar signal. Since then the route has shaved forty years off the deep lane, and three trade cartels levy informal tolls at the northern ring. The liner Vesper of Ruins emerged sixty light-years off-plot in 2288, her passengers two days older than their tickets promised.

The throat has been widening by a few centimeters a season, and no instrument agrees on why. Pilots who transit monthly report dreams of the same unfamiliar coastline, as if the passage remembers them. Convoy masters still pay the tithe, because the alternative is a lifetime of ordinary distance.
